summary: Specifies an automatic tunneling mechanism that lets a service provider deliver IPv6 to customers over its IPv4 network. It uses stateless operation, automatic prefix delegation and simple provisioning. It is a Proposed Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: 6rd lets a provider offer IPv6 to its customers without changing its IPv4 network. Each customer's IPv6 address is built from the provider's own IPv6 prefix plus the customer's IPv4 address, so the tunnel endpoint can be worked out from the address alone, with nothing to keep in a table.

questions: ipv6 over ipv4 tunneling for isps
how does 6rd build an ipv6 prefix
subtitle: How an ISP can hand customers native-looking IPv6 over its existing IPv4 network, with no tunnel state to keep.

tldr.problem: Service providers wanted to give customers IPv6 quickly, but their access networks only carried IPv4 and they wanted to change as little of it as possible.
tldr.mechanism: Customer routers build their IPv6 prefix by combining the provider's 6rd prefix with all or part of their own IPv4 address, then tunnel IPv6 inside IPv4 to other customers or to a Border Relay. The IPv4 address embedded in each IPv6 address tells the sender where the tunnel ends.
tldr.outcome: Customers get IPv6 service equivalent to native IPv6 while the provider keeps running IPv4 unchanged, and 6rd may be discontinued once the network supports native IPv6.

today: RFC 5969 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2010. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updating it. The RFC says 6rd may be discontinued once the provider's network and operations can support fully native IPv6 access and transport.

sections.title: What 6rd Does
sections.content:
6rd specifies a protocol mechanism to deploy IPv6 to sites over a service provider's IPv4 network. It builds on 6to4, with the key differentiator that it uses the provider's own IPv6 address prefix rather than the well-known 2002::/16 prefix. By using that prefix the operational domain of 6rd is limited to the provider's network and is under its direct control, and from the perspective of customer sites and the IPv6 Internet at large the IPv6 service provided is equivalent to native IPv6.

The mechanism relies on an algorithmic mapping between the IPv6 and IPv4 addresses used within the provider's network. That mapping allows the IPv4 tunnel endpoints to be determined automatically from IPv6 prefixes, which allows 6rd to operate statelessly. 6rd views the IPv4 network as a link layer for IPv6 and supports an automatic tunneling abstraction similar to the Non-Broadcast Multiple Access model.

A 6rd domain consists of 6rd Customer Edge routers and one or more 6rd Border Relays. IPv6 packets encapsulated by 6rd follow the IPv4 routing topology inside the provider's network, and the Border Relays are traversed only for packets destined to or arriving from outside the provider's 6rd domain. Because 6rd is stateless, the Border Relays may be reached using anycast for failover and resiliency.

On the customer-facing side of a CE, IPv6 is implemented as it would be for any native IP service, and further IPv6 considerations on that side are out of scope. On the provider-facing side, the WAN interface, encapsulation over Ethernet, ATM or PPP, and control protocols such as PPPoE, IPCP and DHCP all remain unchanged from current IPv4 operation. 6rd is designed to deliver production-quality IPv6 alongside IPv4 with as little change to IPv4 networking and operations as possible, and it uses the same encapsulation and base mechanism as 6to4, so 6to4 could be achieved by setting the 6rd prefix to 2002::/16. Unlike 6to4, 6rd is for use only where a service provider closely manages the delivery of IPv6 service. How the mechanism should be used, and other deployment and operational considerations, are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to leave the existing IPv4 network exactly as it is and carry IPv6 packets inside IPv4 packets across it. Because the provider uses its own address range rather than a shared well-known one, only the provider's own customers can take part.

sections.title: The Pieces
sections.content:
The 6rd prefix is an IPv6 prefix selected by the service provider for use by a 6rd domain, and there is exactly one per domain. A provider may deploy a single domain or several, each with its own prefix.

A 6rd Customer Edge is a device acting as a customer edge router in a 6rd deployment. In a residential broadband deployment this is sometimes called a residential gateway or customer premises equipment. A typical CE serving a residential site has one WAN side interface, one or more LAN side interfaces, and a 6rd virtual interface. The CE WAN side is IPv4-only, while the CE LAN side interface is fully IPv6 enabled.

The 6rd delegated prefix is the IPv6 prefix calculated by the CE for use within the customer site, by combining the 6rd prefix with the CE IPv4 address obtained through IPv4 configuration methods. It can be considered logically equivalent to a DHCPv6 IPv6 delegated prefix.

A 6rd Border Relay is a 6rd-enabled router managed by the provider at the edge of a 6rd domain. It has at least one IPv4-enabled interface, a 6rd virtual interface acting as an endpoint for the IPv6-in-IPv4 tunnel, and an IPv6 interface connected to the native IPv6 network. The BR IPv4 address is the address the CE uses to send packets to a Border Relay in order to reach IPv6 destinations outside the domain.

The 6rd virtual interface is an internal multi-point tunnel interface where the encapsulation and decapsulation of IPv6 packets inside IPv4 takes place. A typical CE or BR implementation needs only one such interface, and a BR in several domains may need more than one, but no more than one per domain. The CE IPv4 address is the address given to the CE as part of normal IPv4 Internet access, and it may be global or private within the domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of box take part. The customer router at the customer's site turns IPv6 into IPv4 and back. The border relay sits at the edge of the provider's network and hands traffic over to the rest of the IPv6 world.

sections.title: How the IPv6 Address Is Built
sections.content:
The 6rd delegated prefix is created by combining the 6rd prefix with all or part of the CE IPv4 address, and the CE creates it automatically when it obtains IPv4 service. It is used in the same manner as a prefix obtained via DHCPv6 prefix delegation.

In 6to4 a similar operation places an entire IPv4 address at a fixed location after a well-known /16 IPv6 prefix. In 6rd the IPv6 prefix, the position of the embedded IPv4 address and the number of bits used all vary from one domain to the next, so the provider can adjust the size of the 6rd prefix, how many bits the mechanism uses, and how many are left for customer sites. To allow stateless address auto-configuration on the CE LAN side, a 6rd delegated prefix SHOULD be /64 or shorter.

The delegated prefix is created by concatenating the 6rd prefix with a consecutive set of bits from the CE IPv4 address, and its length is the length of the 6rd prefix, n, plus the number of IPv4 bits used, o. The remaining bits are used for a subnet ID and an interface ID. For example, if the 6rd prefix is /32 and 24 bits of the CE IPv4 address are used, the delegated prefix for each CE is automatically calculated to be /56.

Embedding fewer than the full 32 bits of a CE IPv4 address is possible only when an aggregated block of IPv4 addresses is available for the domain, which may not be practical with global addresses but is likely where private addresses are used. If private addresses overlap, the deployment may be divided into separate 6rd domains, each addressed with a different 6rd prefix.

Because the delegated prefix is selected algorithmically from the IPv4 address, changing the IPv4 address changes the IPv6 delegated prefix, which would ripple through the site's network. The RFC therefore recommends that the provider assign CE IPv4 addresses with relatively long lifetimes, and that the prefix lifetimes advertised in router advertisements or used by DHCP on the CE LAN side MUST be equal to or shorter than the IPv4 address lease time.
sections.plainLanguage: The address a customer gets is not random. It is the provider's IPv6 prefix with the customer's own IPv4 address stuck into the middle, so the tunnel endpoint can be read straight out of the address. That also means the IPv6 address changes if the IPv4 address changes.

sections.title: The Four Configuration Values
sections.content:
For a given 6rd domain, the BR and the CE MUST be configured with four elements, and the configured values are identical for all CEs and BRs in that domain.

IPv4MaskLen is the number of high-order bits that are identical across all CE IPv4 addresses in the domain. If there are no identical bits, IPv4MaskLen is 0 and the whole IPv4 address is used to build the delegated prefix. If there are 8 identical bits, as with the private range 10.0.0.0/8, IPv4MaskLen is 8 and those high-order bits are stripped from the address before the prefix is constructed. 6rdPrefix is the provider's IPv6 prefix for the domain, and 6rdPrefixLen is its length in bits. 6rdBRIPv4Address is the IPv4 address of the Border Relay for the domain.

The CE values may be set in several ways, including provisioning methods such as the Broadband Forum's TR-69 residential gateway management interface, an XML-based object retrieved after IPv4 connectivity is established, a DNS record, an SMIv2 MIB, PPP IPCP, or manual configuration by an administrator. The RFC describes how to configure the parameters with a single DHCP option. Apart from that, the only information the CE needs in order to calculate the delegated prefix and enable IPv6 connectivity is an IPv4 address for the CE, obtained as part of normal IPv4 Internet access.

A single CE MAY be connected to more than one 6rd domain, and each domain the CE operates within requires its own set of configuration elements and produces its own delegated prefix. The Border Relay MUST be configured with the same elements as the CEs in the same domain. For increased reliability and load balancing, the BR IPv4 address may be an anycast address shared across the domain; since 6rd is stateless, any BR may be used at any time, and if the address is anycast the relay MUST use it as the source address in packets relayed to CEs. Because 6rd uses provider address space, no specific routes need to be advertised externally for 6rd to operate, in either IPv6 or IPv4 BGP, though anycast addresses must be advertised in the provider's IGP.
sections.plainLanguage: Every box in one 6rd domain is told the same four things: how much of the customer's IPv4 address to keep, the provider's IPv6 prefix and its length, and the border relay's IPv4 address. Once that is known, the customer router can work everything else out for itself.

sections.title: The DHCP Option
sections.content:
The 6rd parameters are carried in one DHCPv4 option, OPTION_6RD, with code 212. The option carries the option length, the IPv4MaskLen, the 6rdPrefixLen, the 6rdPrefix as a 16-octet IPv6 address, and one or more IPv4 addresses of the Border Relays.

IPv4MaskLen may be any value between 0 and 32; any value greater than 32 is invalid. For bounds checking by DHCP option processing, the sum of (32 - IPv4MaskLen) and 6rdPrefixLen MUST be less than or equal to 128. The bits in the prefix after the 6rdPrefixLen number of bits are reserved, and MUST be initialized to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver. The option length is 22 octets with one BR IPv4 address, and IANA assigned the option code point with a data length of 18 + N, where N is the number of BR addresses divided by four.

The CE MUST include a Parameter Request List option for OPTION_6RD. Because the option contains one IPv4MaskLen, 6rdPrefixLen and 6rdPrefix block, and DHCP cannot convey more than one instance of an option, OPTION_6RD is limited to provisioning at most a single 6rd domain; provisioning a CE connected to multiple domains is outside the scope of the specification.

The presence of the option indicates that the 6rd service is available. By default, receipt of a valid option by a 6rd-capable CE results in configuration of the 6rd virtual interface and the associated delegated prefix for use on the CE LAN side. The CE MUST be able to configure the 6rd mechanism to be disabled, in which case the option, if received, is silently ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The four values reach the customer router inside a single DHCP option, the same message that normally carries the IPv4 address. A router that is not interested in 6rd simply ignores the option.

sections.title: Checking That the Border Relay Is Reachable
sections.content:
Neighbor unreachability detection for tunnels is described in Section 3.8 of RFC 4213. In 6rd all CEs and BRs can be considered connected to the same virtual link and therefore neighbours of each other, and this section describes how to use neighbor unreachability detection without harming the scalability of a deployment.

A typical 6rd deployment may have a very large number of CEs in the same domain, and reachability between CEs is based on IPv4 routing. Sending neighbor unreachability detection or any periodic packets between 6rd CE devices beyond isolated troubleshooting is NOT RECOMMENDED. Reachability detection between a given CE and BR is not necessary for 6rd to work, but where a CE has alternative paths to the BR it could be useful. Periodic messages from a very large number of CEs could overload the BR control message processing path, so a CE that needs to determine BR reachability MUST use a method that lets the reachability detection packets follow a typical data forwarding path without special processing by the BR.

The method described works like this. The CE constructs a payload of any size and content, and encapsulates it with an inner IPv6 and outer IPv4 header. The IPv6 destination address is set to an address from the CE's own 6rd delegated prefix that is assigned to a virtual interface, and the IPv6 source address is set to an address from the same prefix, the same one as the destination. The IPv4 header is then added as it normally would be for any packet destined for the BR, with the BR as the IPv4 destination and the CE IPv4 address as the source. The CE sends the packet out of the interface on which BR reachability is being monitored. On successful receipt the BR MUST decapsulate and forward the packet normally, which sends it back to the CE through the 6rd mechanism. Arrival of the packet at the CE's IPv6 address completes one round trip without the BR processing the message outside its normal data forwarding path. The payload may be empty or carry values meaningful to the CE, and its format is left to the implementer.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no need to keep checking whether the border relay is there, and doing so with thousands of customers would overload it. If a check is wanted, the customer router sends an ordinary data packet to itself through the relay, and the relay handles it like any other packet.

sections.title: Encapsulation, Packet Size and Receiving Rules
sections.content:
IPv6 in IPv4 encapsulation and forwarding manipulations, such as handling packet markings and checksumming, are performed as specified in Section 3.5 of RFC 4213, the same mechanism used by 6to4. ICMPv4 errors are handled as specified in Section 3.4 of that document. By default the IPv6 Traffic Class field MUST be copied to the IPv4 ToS field, though this default MAY be overridden by configuration. IPv6 packets from a CE are encapsulated in IPv4 packets when they leave the site via the CE WAN side interface.

The 6rd link is modeled as an NBMA link, with all CEs and BRs defined as off-link neighbours of one another. No communication using link-local addresses occurs.

On maximum transmission unit, IPv4 path MTU discovery MAY be used to adjust the MTU of the tunnel, or the 6rd tunnel MTU may be configured explicitly. Using an anycast source address could lead to an ICMP error message generated on the path being sent to a different Border Relay, so the use of dynamic tunnel MTU is subject to IPv4 path MTU blackholes. Multiple BRs using the same anycast source address could send fragmented packets to the same CE at the same time, and if the fragments from different BRs happen to use the same fragment ID, incorrect reassembly might occur; for that reason a BR using an anycast source address MUST set the IPv4 Don't Fragment flag. If the IPv4 MTU on the CE WAN side is known, the 6rd tunnel MTU should be set to that MTU minus the size of the encapsulating IPv4 header, which is 20 bytes, so an IPv4 MTU of 1500 bytes would give a tunnel MTU of 1480 bytes. Absent more specific information, the 6rd tunnel MTU SHOULD default to 1280 bytes.

The receiving rules exist to prevent spoofing of IPv6 addresses. The BR and the CE MUST validate the embedded IPv4 source address of an encapsulated IPv6 packet against the IPv4 source address it is encapsulated by, according to the configured parameters of the domain. If the two do not match, the packet MUST be dropped and a counter incremented to indicate that a spoofing attack may be under way. A CE MUST also allow forwarding of packets sourced by the configured BR IPv4 address. By default the CE router MUST drop packets received on the 6rd virtual interface for IPv6 destinations outside its own 6rd delegated prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: Each IPv6 packet travels inside an IPv4 packet, so the tunnel is smaller than the link underneath it. The router also checks that the IPv4 address hidden inside the IPv6 address matches the one that carried it, which is what stops someone forging an address from another customer.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A 6to4 relay router can be used as an open relay, relaying IPv6 traffic and acting as a traffic anonymizer. By restricting the 6rd domain to within a provider's network, a CE only needs to accept packets from a single or small set of known Border Relay IPv4 addresses, so many of the threats described against 6to4 in RFC 3964 do not apply. When the receiving rules are applied, IPv6 packets are as well protected against spoofing as IPv4 packets are within the provider's network.

A malicious user who knows a 6rd domain and the BR IPv4 address could construct a packet that causes a Border Relay to reflect tunneled packets outside the domain it serves, and with an IPv6 source address that looks as if it came from another 6rd domain, forwarding loops between 6rd domains may be created, allowing a packet amplification attack between domains. One mitigation is simply not to allow the BR IPv4 address to be reachable from outside the provider's 6rd domain: carefully constructed packets could still be reflected off a single BR, but the looping condition would not occur, and tunneled packets with the BR IPv4 address as the source address could also be filtered.

To avoid forwarding loops via other internal relays, the BR should use outgoing and incoming IPv4 packet filters, filtering out all known relay addresses for internal 6rd BRs, ISATAP routers or 6to4 relays, including the well-known anycast address space for 6to4. The BR MUST install a null route for its own 6rd delegated prefix, created from its BR IPv4 address, with the exception of the IPv6 Subnet-Router anycast address.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the mechanism only works inside one provider's network, most of the well-known 6to4 attacks do not apply. The remaining risk is a crafted packet that makes two providers bounce traffic back and forth, and the RFC says how to filter that.
